body:
Digital twins: a virtual representation connected to a real system

A digital twin is a digital representation of a physical object, process or system that is connected to information about the corresponding real system. Information from sensors, operating records or other sources can update the representation as the real system changes.

For example, a factory may maintain a digital twin of a production machine. The virtual representation can use information such as temperature, operating speed, vibration or production output to reflect the machine's condition. Engineers may examine the information to understand performance, identify abnormal behaviour or assess possible operational changes.

A digital twin is not necessarily a realistic 3D picture. Its essential value is the relationship between the physical system and the digital information used to represent its condition or behaviour.

Digital model, simulation and digital twin

A digital model may show how an object has been designed. A simulation can estimate how a model behaves under specified conditions. A digital twin goes further by maintaining a meaningful connection with information from the real system.

A computer model does not automatically become a digital twin simply because it looks like the actual machine. The information must be sufficiently relevant and updated for the intended use. Depending on the application, updates may be continuous, frequent or periodic; a digital twin does not have to receive every sensor reading instantaneously.

Digital twins can assist with monitoring, diagnosis, prediction and planning. Their usefulness depends on data quality and the accuracy of the representation. Incorrect measurements or unsuitable assumptions may produce misleading conclusions.

Additive manufacturing: producing objects layer by layer

Additive manufacturing builds a 3-dimensional object by adding material according to a digital design. It is commonly associated with 3D printing.

A simplified process begins with a digital model of the intended part. Manufacturing software prepares instructions for successive layers. A suitable machine adds or solidifies material in those layers until the object is formed. Different additive processes can use plastics, metals or other materials.

Additive manufacturing is useful for producing prototypes, customised parts and some geometrically complex components. It can reduce material waste in certain applications because material is placed where needed rather than being removed from a large starting block.

Additive and subtractive manufacturing

In subtractive manufacturing, material is removed from a larger workpiece by methods such as cutting, drilling or milling. In additive manufacturing, the object is built by adding material.

Neither approach is always superior. Additive manufacturing can provide flexibility for complex or customised parts, while conventional manufacturing methods may be faster or less expensive for particular materials, simple shapes or high-volume production.

A digital twin is used to represent and analyse a physical system. Additive manufacturing is used to produce a physical object from a digital design. The 2 technologies can support the same factory without performing the same function.

Predictive maintenance: acting before equipment fails

Industrial machines require maintenance to remain safe and reliable. Maintenance decisions can be based on a failure that has already occurred, a fixed schedule or information suggesting that a failure may be approaching.

ApproachWhen maintenance occursExample
Reactive maintenanceAfter a breakdown or failure.Repairing a motor after it stops working.
Preventive maintenanceAt a planned time or operating interval.Inspecting equipment after a set number of operating hours.
Predictive maintenanceWhen monitored conditions indicate an increasing likelihood of failure.Planning an inspection after vibration trends suggest bearing deterioration.

How predictive maintenance works

Suppose a rotating machine normally operates with a low level of vibration. Over several weeks, a sensor records a rising vibration trend. The monitoring system identifies an abnormal change. Based on that condition and the machine's operating history, maintenance personnel may determine that a bearing needs inspection or replacement before the machine stops.

Measurements such as vibration, temperature, noise and operating conditions can support this type of maintenance. Predictive systems may use statistical analysis, learned patterns or other suitable methods; advanced artificial intelligence is not essential in every application.

Condition-based maintenance and predictive maintenance overlap but are not always identical. Condition-based maintenance responds to observed equipment condition, while predictive maintenance seeks to anticipate deterioration or failure using that information.

Predictive maintenance can reduce avoidable downtime and unnecessary maintenance in suitable circumstances. However, sensors can fail, warning signals can be misleading and not every breakdown can be predicted. Skilled inspection and engineering judgement remain important.

How these technologies can work together

A digitally connected factory may monitor machines through sensors, use a digital twin to analyse their performance and schedule maintenance using observed trends. The factory might also use additive manufacturing to produce selected prototypes or replacement components when the materials, quality requirements and economics make it appropriate.

These technologies are complementary rather than interchangeable. Each solves a different industrial problem.

Prelims focus

  • A digital twin is a data-connected representation of a physical system.
  • A static 3D model is not automatically a digital twin.
  • Additive manufacturing builds objects layer by layer from a digital design.
  • Subtractive manufacturing removes material from a workpiece.
  • Predictive maintenance uses observed data to anticipate possible equipment failure.
  • Trap: Scheduled preventive maintenance and data-based predictive maintenance are not identical.

[NIST, Digital Twins for Advanced Manufacturing, Summary, virtual representations and operational uses; NIST, Digital Manufacturing: Requirements and Challenges for Implementing Digital Surrogates, abstract, 12 December 2018; NIST, What Is Additive Manufacturing?, Summary and manufacturing definition; NIST, Additive Manufacturing FAQs, operating principle and applications; NIST, Manufacturing Machinery Maintenance, maintenance-type definitions; online sources consulted 5 November 2026.]

title: Industry 4.0 Technologies: Digital Twins, Additive Manufacturing and Predictive Maintenance

body:
How semiconductors support Industry 4.0

Semiconductor technology and Industry 4.0 are closely connected, but they describe different levels of technology. The semiconductor industry designs and produces electronic components. Industry 4.0 uses electronic components, software and communication systems to organise physical manufacturing processes more effectively.

A sensor in an industrial machine may contain semiconductor devices that help convert a physical condition into an electrical signal. A microcontroller or processor can interpret that information, while power-electronic components can help control motors or other equipment. Memory chips can store operating information, and communication chips can transfer data between connected devices.

Thus, semiconductor devices are important enabling components of cyber-physical systems. The larger system also depends on software, mechanical equipment, communication arrangements, electrical power and appropriate human supervision.

An example from industrial electricity use

Consider an industrial motor that operates a pump. Sensors can measure the motor's temperature, current or vibration. A controller may issue an alarm when conditions become abnormal. If authorised automatic control is provided, it may also adjust operation or initiate a safe shutdown.

Maintenance personnel can examine recorded data to decide whether the equipment needs attention. This illustrates how semiconductor-based sensors and controllers can support cyber-physical monitoring and predictive maintenance. The presence of sensors alone does not guarantee that every system can predict failures or operate autonomously.

Changes in the industrial workforce

Industrial automation changes the tasks performed by workers. Repetitive or physically demanding activities may increasingly be performed by machines. At the same time, connected industrial systems create or expand the need for workers who can operate, maintain, inspect and improve those systems.

Skills required across the ecosystem

  • Semiconductor design: Understanding electronic circuits and using suitable chip-design tools.
  • Fabrication and packaging: Operating manufacturing equipment, maintaining process quality and checking finished components.
  • Industrial automation: Understanding sensors, controllers, actuators and machine safety.
  • Data interpretation: Recognising abnormal operating conditions and using measurements to support decisions.
  • Maintenance: Combining equipment knowledge with monitoring information and inspection.
  • Cybersecurity and safety: Protecting connected equipment and ensuring that control failures do not create unsafe conditions.

These changes create opportunities for specialised employment, but they also require reskilling and upskilling. Workers whose former tasks are automated may need training for new roles. The effects on employment depend on the industry, adoption rate, available training and organisation of work; automation does not produce the same outcome in every workplace.

India's programme for smart manufacturing

SAMARTH Udyog Bharat 4.0 is an initiative of the Ministry of Heavy Industries intended to promote awareness, demonstration and adoption of Industry 4.0 technologies in Indian manufacturing.

Its activities involve demonstration and support facilities associated with institutions such as the Centre for Industry 4.0 (C4i4) in Pune, the IIT Delhi-AIA Foundation for Smart Manufacturing, IISc Bengaluru and the Central Manufacturing Technology Institute (CMTI). These facilities support understanding, testing and adoption of smart-manufacturing methods.

This programme has a different primary focus from ISM. ISM supports development of the semiconductor and display ecosystem, whereas SAMARTH Udyog Bharat 4.0 promotes the use of advanced digital technologies in manufacturing. The two areas reinforce one another but are not the same programme.

Benefits and limitations of connected industry

Potential benefits

  • Better monitoring of equipment condition and production quality.
  • Earlier identification of some faults and avoidable stoppages.
  • More responsive production scheduling and material use.
  • Improved consistency in tasks suited to automated control.
  • Greater opportunities for specialised design, maintenance and technical services.

Important limitations and risks

  • Cybersecurity: Connected machines may be exposed to unauthorised access, manipulation or disruption.
  • Data reliability: Incorrect sensor readings may cause inappropriate alarms or decisions.
  • Compatibility: Machines and software from different suppliers may not communicate easily.
  • Cost and skills: New equipment, maintenance and workforce training require investment.
  • Safety: Automatic control needs suitable safeguards and clearly defined human responsibility.
  • Resource and environmental impact: Semiconductor manufacturing and digital systems consume materials and energy, while electronic products create end-of-life waste-management requirements.

For smaller manufacturers, the appropriate solution may be a limited monitoring or automation improvement rather than immediate conversion to a fully connected factory. Technology should be selected according to the problem being solved and the expected benefit.

Putting the complete subtopic together

The overall relationship begins with semiconductor materials, whose electrical behaviour can be controlled. Engineers use these materials to make chips through design, fabrication, packaging and testing. Chips support the sensors, controllers, memory and communications used in cyber-physical systems.

When these systems are connected to industrial production, they can support Industry 4.0. Digital twins, condition monitoring and predictive maintenance help interpret equipment behaviour, while additive manufacturing provides an additional way of producing selected physical parts.

India's semiconductor programmes seek to strengthen the supply of electronic components and the skills needed to produce them. Smart-manufacturing programmes seek to help industries use digital and automation technologies effectively. Both are relevant to manufacturing capability, employment and technological development.

Prelims focus

  • Semiconductor chips support sensing, processing, memory, communication and electrical control.
  • Cyber-physical systems combine electronic computation with real physical processes.
  • Digital twins support digital representation and analysis; predictive maintenance uses equipment-condition information.
  • Industry 4.0 changes workforce skill requirements and increases the importance of cybersecurity and machine safety.
  • SAMARTH Udyog Bharat 4.0 is an initiative of the Ministry of Heavy Industries.
  • Trap: India Semiconductor Mission and SAMARTH Udyog Bharat 4.0 serve related but different industrial purposes.
